#2619. Brewers' Pat Murphy apologized to Yankees' Brian Cashman over viral comment about Jake Bauers free agency

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In the aftermath of the World Series championship, Brewers manager Pat Murphy was caught on a hot mic talking to first baseman and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, who heads into free agency this winter off a career year.

Murphy's message? "You're gonna be a rich f---er, but just remember when you were on that horseshit Yankees team and you guys were all playing for yourself, just remember, say, 'this is the way we used to do it.'"

The comment, predictably, drew backlash from those who assumed Murphy was taking a shot at the Yankees. Bauers was on the 2023 Yankees, when they went 82-80 and missed the playoffs.

"I called Brian Cashman right away when I heard it got out," Murphy said on the New York Post's "The Show with Joel Sherman and Jon Heyman released on Tuesday. "I picked up a phone and called Brian right away, and had a good conversation. And the best I could try to explain that I wasn't talking about the 2026 Yankees.

"After every celebration, I'd shake his hand. I'd say, 'You rich so-and-so, you're going to leave us,' " Murphy explained. "We're not going to be able to pay you. You're going to leave us and you're going to forget all about how we did things. … I would just give him this rhetoric every time.

"I was just referring to the teams that have a lot of high-paid, long-contract players," Murphy said. "That sometimes it's harder to get all those guys together to play together. And I used the Yankees because I knew Jake was with them before. … I regret saying it, but that was Jake and I's humor behind the scenes and I got caught."

First off, dudes talking to dudes when they don't realize anyone else is listening lends itself to a lot of comments they don't necessarily mean or, perhaps more importantly, don't include the context of a longstanding relationship between a manager and his player. There isn't anything really out of line here in terms of the Yankees shot. Any Yankees fan would tell you they agree with Murphy's assessment of that team.

Where I do believe there's a problem is the insinuation that a player getting a huge payday means that he'll just start playing only for himself instead of doing things as a team. The Dodgers' high individual salaries certainly didn't stop them from winning two straight World Series titles.

Further, Bauers made $2.7 million last season, double his previous high. MLB players have a finite shelf life and need the money they make to stretch, if they're lucky, for generations. He's set to make exponentially more in free agency in his one big payday to hopefully set up his family for decades. Some might think it insensitive of Murphy to mock that a player might need to look out for himself and his family.

Then again, take note of Murphy's quote when he says that's just their sense of humor. We don't know their personal relationship because it is just that: personal. Unless Bauers signs elsewhere and comes out guns blazing against Murphy, this whole thing is probably just much ado about nothing. It would be pretty shocking if Cashman took particular offense, either.

#2616. Former Yankees, Rangers All-Star Mark Teixeira wins U.S. House seat in Texas

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former Major League Baseball star Mark Teixeira is headed to Capitol Hill after winning the election for the United States House of Representatives seat in Texas' 21st district on Tuesday. Teixeira, the Republican candidate, beat Democrat Kristin Hook, a former federal scientist.

Teixeira will now take over the seat vacated by Republican Chip Roy, who didn't seek re-election.

"Together, we can build a better future for our families, our neighbors, and every community across Texas 21," Teixeira said in a statement. "I'm excited to get to work. I will be praying for all of you and for the future of this great nation. God bless Texas, and God bless America."

He was a rare win for the GOP in Texas on Tuesday, as Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the gubernatorial race and Democrat James Talarico flipped the Senate seat.

Teixeira, 46, was born and raised in Maryland before attending Georgia Tech as a big-time prospect. He was selected fifth overall in the first round of the 2001 Draft by the Rangers. He then came up through the Rangers' system and spent the first four and a half seasons of his career with the ballclub. He was traded to the Braves in 2007, then to the Angels in 2008 before signing a long-term free agent deal with the Yankees prior to the 2009 season. He finished his career with the Yankees.

In parts of 14 seasons, Teixeira hit .268/.360/.509 (126 OPS+) with 409 home runs, 1,298 RBI, five Gold Gloves, three All-Star Games, three Silver Sluggers and a World Series ring.

Teixeira is one of several familiar sports faces up for election on Tuesday. Former college football coach Tommy Tuberville won the Alabama gubernatorial race and former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya lost the Minnesota Senate race.

#2613. MLB rumors: The only Oriole not on the trading block, Rays' Drew Rasmussen plan and Astros add to manager hunt

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Brewers have now been World Series champions for just one week (minus a few hours) and they should still be basking in the glory for quite a while. As the offseason marches on, the next big date will be Nov. 17, when decisions on qualifying offers are due from the eight players who received one.

In the meantime, the rumor mill should be ever-so-slowly churning. We'll round it up here.

The Houston Astros moved on from general manager Dana Brown in August and fired manager Joe Espada after the 2026 season. Newly hired general manager Randy Flores is now tasked with landing a new dugout boss, and a three-time MVP and future Hall of Famer is in the mix. The Astros will interview Albert Pujols for the manager job this week, per The Athletic.

Pujols has long made it known that he desires to be an MLB manager. He recently interviewed for vacancies with the Padres and Angels (both last offseason) and he also managed the Dominican Republic in the World Baseball Classic this past spring. It should be further noted that Pujols is in the fourth year of a 10-year, $100 personal services contract with the Angels that was part of the mega-deal he signed with them as a player prior to the 2012 season as a player.

Other known candidates for the Astros manager job are Rangers bench coach Luis Urueta and Yankees bench coach (not to mention former Tigers and Angels manager) Brad Ausmus. Former Astros third baseman Morgan Ensberg, the manager of the Triple-A Rays affiliate Durham Bulls, will also interview this week, according to MLB.com.

The Orioles are willing to listen to trade offers on any player other than Pete Alonso as they seek both rotation and outfield help, according to The Baltimore Banner. The  Orioles reportedly aren't "actively shopping" any players, but they are looking for upgrades at starting pitcher and outfielder and realize one of the ways that could happen is via a trade.

Surely they wouldn't sell low on Gunnar Henderson, given his immense upside, so we can probably take him off the table unless some team makes it worth their while. There is a glut of infielders, though. With Alonso at first base and Henderson at short, they have Jackson Holliday, Christian Encarnacion-Strand, Jordan Westburg and Coby Mayo for two spots. Even using one of the four at designated hitter, it's easy to see where a deal could happen.

Westburg and Encarnacion-Strand are under team control through 2029 while Holliday is controlled through 2030 and Mayo through 2031.

The American League champion Rays recently picked up the $20 million club option on All-Star starting pitcher Drew Rasmussen. That would be a franchise-record salary for one player in a single season. It might seem odd to exercise an option and then deal a player to an outsider, but locking Rasmussen in for a one-year deal makes him an attractive trade candidate instead of just letting him walk in free agency, and this is how the Rays generally operate. We've seen it so many times: they get ahead of losing guys to free agency, sometimes even dealing them a year or two earlier. They've done it with Randy Arozarena, Isaac Paredes, Tyler Glasnow and even going back to franchise legends like David Price, Evan Longoria and Ben Zobrist.

The Rays right now are saying they intend to keep Rasmussen for 2027.

"Not a declarative this, that, whatever, but I can sit here very confidently and say that every intention right now is thinking about Ras anchoring our rotation and how to make this team better going into next year," club president Erik Neander said on Tuesday, via the Tampa Bay Times.

If they want to contend again next year, it sure seems like they need Rasmussen, with Nick Martinez and Freddy Peralta off to free agency. That leaves Rasmussen atop the rotation, followed by Shane McClanahan, Griffin Jax, Ryan Pepiot and a bunch of question marks. There are questions attached to McClanahan, Jax and Pepiot too.

The NBA probably has been my favorite professional sports league since Michael Jordan's Bulls started dominating. Long time, I know. But I've been pulling back that interest some in recent years because I am so tired of healthy guys sitting out for "rest management." These guys only work seven months a year and make lifetime money. If you are hurt, that's hugely different.

In my opinion, the Pacers embarrassed themselves and the NBA on Monday in a 108-104 home loss to Atlanta, Indiana's fifth straight loss. Yes, some guys were out injured for the team in that one but 11 guys were out -- representing about 93% of their payroll – with six total available.  All six guys — including the team's three two-way players — played 34 or more minutes and reached double figures. Second-round rookie guard Braden Smith, so good in college at Purdue, had a double-double with 19 points and 10 assists in 42 minutes of action.

Per NBA.com, it marked the first time in 22 years that the Pacers used so few players in a game. While it was the eighth instance of teams using only six guys over the past 15 seasons, almost all the others were in meaningless games at the end of the campaign when teams are tanking or resting for the playoffs. This season isn't even two weeks old.

The last time a team used only six players in a game even in the first month of season was on Nov. 24, 2009, when Golden State did and still beat Dallas. ESPN topped that stat by telling me that the last time a team used six or fewer players this early in a season was in 1948, when the Lakers used five in their third game of the season.

What really irked me was Indiana resting arguably its second-best player in Pascal Siakam in the second of a back-to-back when the roster was in such bad shape. Kelly Oubre Jr. was a late scratch because of a bruised knee and Larry Nance Jr. sat with an illness.

Now, some guys are truly hurt and also won't play tonight: Superstar Tyrese Haliburton and fellow guards TJ McConnell, Ben Sheppard and Johnny Furphy. But Oubre, fellow forward Obi Toppin and starting center Ivica Zubac are all questionable after also sitting. Zubac would be a help, as he has been limited to only three games and has not played since Oct. 25. So I expect a competitive team tonight but one that also might be looking ahead to its next game against Denver in Mexico City on Saturday.

My plan here was to focus on huge surprise Memphis, which is near the top of the Western Conference at 6-1 and was the league's last to lose despite a preseason win total set at just 28.5, which was among the NBA's lowest.

This was to be a full-on rebuilding season behind No. 3 overall rookie Cameron Boozer. The former Duke star has been great, to the point that maybe Washington at No. 1 (AJ Dybantsa) and Utah at No. 2 (Darryn Peterson) already realize they made a mistake passing on Boozer.

He's your +200 favorite for NBA Rookie of the Year and just plays so much wiser than his 19 years of age in averaging 17.4 points, 10.3 rebounds and 5.6 assists. He had an 18/12/12 triple-double in a very impressive win in Portland on Oct. 29, becoming the youngest front-court player in league annals with one.  Just think how good he'll be when he bulks up and starts shooting better – only 36% from the field so far. For tonight, Booser has an Over/Under PRA of 32.5.

That's tied for second-highest tonight with Siakam (33.5), along with maybe the NBA's most surprising player in Grizzlies 29-year-old journeyman guard Ty Jerome. He's averaging a stunning 28.2 points per game on 50.4% from the field. That's obviously not going to be sustained for someone who doesn't even average double-digit points for his career – although he scored a career-high 19.7 PPG last season.

I thought Jerome's fade already had started with just 25 points in back-to-back games before putting up 40 in that first loss of the year Monday, 135-134 in OT vs. New Orleans. The Grizzlies are listing reserve guard Scotty Pippen Jr. (6.4 PPG) as out and backup center Quentin Post (7.6 PPG) as questionable.

The Pacers have lost five straight games in Memphis, with their last win there on April 11, 2021. The model expects that trend to continue with a 121-118 Grizzlies victory. Indiana is decently defensively at 115.8 PPG, and Zubac will help on that end. Check out other expert picks in the SportsLine daily newsletter.

#2611. 2026 NFL trade deadline: One realistic, one pipe dream trade scenario for every playoff contender

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NFL trade deadline is less than a week away, and every team is in position to either put themselves over the top in hopes of a playoff push, or to completely reset their franchise and move on to NFL Draft season.

We've already seen big names like LG Quenton Nelson and DTs DeForest Buckner and Jeffrey Simmons getting dealt before the deadline. And I get the feeling that more big names will be on the move once we get to November 10.

For every team in the current playoff picture, we'll break down one realistic trade and one pipe dream trade they can make to put themselves over the top, in addition to a few interesting ones outside of the playoff mix.

Pipe Dream Trade: Jessie Bates, S, Atlanta Falcons

Realistic Trade: Amani Hooker, S, Tennessee Titans

The Bills have gotten more than enough from their defensive front, a unit that I thought would come along slowly in the beginning of the season. EDGE Greg Rousseau is playing at a DPOY-caliber level, and the emergence of DT Deone Walker has helped their defensive line gain some teeth. However, the Bills have given up the fifth-most completions of 20+ yards in the NFL this season and lack impact play from their secondary.

Cornerback is a spot where they could improve, but they have a lot of faith in rookie CB Davison Igbinosun opposite Christian Benford. However, the safety spot opposite Cole Bishop could use some improvement. While most people will point to Arizona Cardinals' safety Budda Baker as the top target, he and Bishop's skillsets overlap.

Bates is entering the final year of his contract with the Falcons, and he has been an impact player when the ball is in the air and when separating the ball from the player (three PBUs, one INT and three forced fumbles in 2026). Bates is the perfect complement to Bishop and could help tilt the scales back in the Bills' favor.

Hooker makes a lot of sense as a realistic target for the Bills. There's some freedom in his contract as he enters the final two years of his 2025 deal, but he's a reliable post safety who can complement Bishop's skills closer to the line of scrimmage.

Pipe Dream Trade: RB Jonathan Taylor, Indianapolis Colts

Realistic Trade: TE Dallas Goedert, Philadelphia Eagles

I wouldn't be surprised if the Broncos ultimately stand pat at the deadline, after all the rumors and whispers that they're looking for something big. With the emergence of RB Jonah Coleman in this offense, the Denver running game has found some new life to go along with the mandatory second-half Bo Nix resurgence.

However, if the Broncos were looking to make a big swing, it would obviously be for Colts' RB Jonathan Taylor. While Coleman has been very good, the explosiveness Taylor would bring makes a pedestrian Broncos offense more dangerous from anywhere on the field (since 2023, Taylor has 78 explosive runs, 5th-most in the NFL). This season, Denver is 26th in Explosive Play Rate, behind teams like the Philadelphia Eagles and the Tennessee Titans, and offense gets really hard when you can't generate explosives. Taylor is not only a big-play machine but would also loosen some of the constraints on the Denver offense as they try to make the Super Bowl.

Now, for a realistic trade scenario, I do think the Broncos look at other positions. I doubt they'd be able to get him from within the division, but LB Daiyan Henley could really give the Broncos' defense a nitro boost. However, I'm eyeing Eagles' TE Dallas Goedert as a realistic trade target.

The Broncos have gotten next to nothing out of their tight end group this year (second-lowest receiving yards to TEs this season, per TruMedia). Goedert is entering the final year of his contract with the Eagles. He would give the Broncos a reliable player down the seams and a competitive blocker who wouldn't be an obvious tell when he's on the field.

Pipe Dream Trade: WR Josh Downs, Indianapolis Colts

Realistic Trade: CB Amik Robertson, Washington Commanders

The Steelers have surprisingly found themselves at the top of the AFC North behind an offense that's gone fully into bullyball, but at the deadline I think adding a receiver with some separation skills could really give the Pittsburgh passing offense some juice. The Steelers have struggled this season throwing against man coverage, ranking 25th in EPA per play and 30th in Success Rate on all dropbacks against man coverage. DK Metcalf hasn't inspired much confidence in the receiver room, and despite the emergence of rookie Germie Bernard, the room overall doesn't have much teeth.

Enter Josh Downs, who is the exact receiver this version of the Steelers needs. Since 2023, among all players with 175 total targets, Downs is 13th in the NFL in percentage of receptions  (80.4%) against man coverage that go for first downs or touchdowns. While he's more of a slot receiver, he's a guy who can win with crafty route running and acceleration in and out of breaks. QB Aaron Rodgers loves throwing sight adjustments and option slants to receivers when he sees the number count in his favor, but those haven't worked with Metcalf. Downs can win on those and give the Steelers an easy button in their passing game.

Their most realistic option could be on the other side of the ball, however. The Steelers' secondary needs more speed and urgency, and no two words embody Amik Robertson more. The Commanders' CB plays with zero fear and has inside/outside versatility, giving DC Patrick Graham options with the cornerback room. Robertson also has experience with Graham from his time in Las Vegas. He feels like an easy and reliable candidate for Pittsburgh to go after.

The Jaguars were in the market for more interior help even before the injury to DT Davon Hamilton, but with Hamilton out for the rest of the season the need for the Jaguars to add there becomes increasingly important. Even with some of the need at safety, Hamilton was a massive part of why the Jaguars were so good in run defense. Losing him puts a significant chunk into what they want to be defensively, and I think the Jaguars will want to replace his spot as they get ready to make a deep playoff run. On top of that, the Jaguars' pass rush production from the interior has been lacking, with rotational DT Ruke Orhorhoro leading the group in pressure rate at 11.2%. Getting more productivity from the group is paramount.

There are plenty of names that stand out as trade options at DT, but I think the biggest fish they could get is Barmore, a productive and imposing pass rusher who might be on his way out of New England. The Pats have gotten good play from their rotational guys such as Cory Durden and Leonard Taylor, and while Barmore has been a very good pass rusher, the Pats could see him as expendable. Barmore leads the Patriots in total pressures since 2025, and his 11.8% pressure rate since 2025 would be the best on the Jaguars in that same time period. Barmore's presence would make Jaguars' EDGEs Josh Hines-Allen and Travon Walker's jobs easier as pass rushers as well.

If they miss out on Barmore, Zach Sieler would be a nice consolation for a cheaper price. The Dolphins are looking more towards 2027, and Sieler doesn't seem to be in the plans for the Dolphins' youth movement going forward. Sieler had a down year last season, but he's a hard charging DT who wins with effort and has 16 pressures in seven games so far. He would take the load off of Hines-Allen and Walker, and while not providing as much pop as Barmore, he would be another quality piece added to the Jags' pass rush.

Pipe Dream Trade: WR Garrett Wilson, New York Jets

Realistic Trade: WR Brian Thomas Jr., Jacksonville Jaguars

Are you sensing a theme with the Chiefs? Kansas City has been looking for help since Tyreek Hill left, and this season has been one of the most dire for the receiving group. With WR Tyquan Thornton out for an extended period of time, the Chiefs need more explosive capability and winners against man coverage.

Travis Kelce leads the Chiefs in explosive receptions with 10, and Tyquan Thornton is still tied for the lead in that category among the receivers. He's tied with WR Xavier Worthy, but Worthy hasn't proven himself to be reliable downfield or in high-leverage situations. The Chiefs need some more talent in the receiving room and should be aggressive in making a move at the deadline for it.

I'm not sure if the Jets would be willing to part with Wilson, but if there's any pie-in-the-sky trade the Chiefs could make, it would be for Wilson. He's an urgent and explosive route runner who can create separation at all three levels and give the Chiefs an actual legit WR1. He would also allow for the Kansas City offense to slide receivers like Rice and Worthy down the pecking order, where Rice can be a winner on over routes and insert as a Z and movement receiver, while Worthy can be the designer downfield target player.

While not on the same level as Garrett Wilson, Brian Thomas Jr. could be a more realistic option for Kansas City if they want to create explosives. The Jaguars seem to want Thomas Jr. around in their offense, but if the right price were offered, Thomas Jr. would give the Chiefs an actual vertical threat in their offense that they won't have with Thornton out.

Thomas Jr. sometimes has issues with focus drops and route depth, but he can win outside the numbers on go routes, corners, and out routes, and he has enough size for Mahomes to feel confident throwing the ball to him. Thomas Jr. might not be a WR1, but he would fill a role that the Chiefs desperately need.

Pipe Dream Trade: LB Daiyan Henley, Los Angeles Chargers

Realistic Trade: CB Riq Woolen, Philadelphia Eagles

With the Bengals' offense looking like one of the best units in the NFL, the Bengals can start adding more to a defensive unit that has shown really high highs, but also some really catastrophic lows. Cincinnati has spent a lot on the defensive line, and it's paid off (DT Dexter Lawrence is a legitimate DPOY candidate), but the linebacker and secondary rooms could need some major work.

The linebacker room especially needs to improve; the unit as a whole has given up the 13th-most yards per coverage snap among all LB groups in the NFL and the seventh-highest positive play rate allowed among all LB groups. In the secondary, star CB DJ Turner is nursing an injury, and Cincinnati could use some more juice from the cornerback room to allow CB Dax Hill to play nickel, where he's at his best.

To address the LB position, Henley would be a hand-in-glove fit for what the Bengals are looking for. The Chargers might not be in the mood to sell anyone, but with Henley not yet getting an extension from LA, it could be time for both to part ways. Henley is an urgent player who can fix the Bengals' gaps in pass coverage and thrive as a blitzer, getting downhill to make plays. In Al Golden's defense, he'll provide an immediate upgrade to the linebacker group the Bengals are trotting out right now.

Woolen is a little volatile, but he also would give the Bengals some big-play capability at cornerback and the ability to move Hill back inside to the slot. He hasn't been his best this season in Philadelphia, but in a defense that allows him to exclusively play the vertical plane, he could get back to top form.

Pipe Dream Trade: EDGE Alex Highsmith, Pittsburgh Steelers

Realistic Trade: EDGE Will McDonald IV, New York Jets

The Patriots find themselves in a really fascinating situation, where most of their impact players are injured, but could be back before the playoffs. Left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker is going to be back this season after being put on IR, as will WR AJ Brown. Maybe a trade for another offensive lineman like Eagles' guard Landon Dickerson would help this offense (Vera-Tucker moves to right guard in this scenario), but reshuffling the deck chairs like that could cause a lot of crossed wires.

Defensively, however, the Patriots could stand to add some different types of players to their pass rush room. EDGE Elijah Ponder has been a revelation, and rookie Gabe Jacas as well as free agent addition Dre'Mont Jones have added more physicality to the room. However, they could add some more players with speed and burst to the building. Harold Landry III hasn't played, and head coach Mike Vrabel hasn't given any clear return date, meaning it's more likely than not that Landry will not play this season. Adding a speed-based pass rusher to the room could allow for the Pats to vary up their approaches and keep offenses guessing.

The Steelers also have a fascinating problem on their hands. While they do sit at the top of the division, they have three highly paid EDGE rushers who can't all play together. Looking across the board, Highsmith's contract is the most tradeable, and he could recoup some nice value for the Steelers. Highsmith is the exact type of player New England needs, explosive upfield with a variety of ways to get to the QB, including a wicked spin move. It'll cost a little bit more than expected, but Highsmith would give the Patriots EDGE room some much-needed juice.

Lower down the totem pole, Jets' EDGE Will McDonald IV looms as a trade target. Another guy who wins with speed and inside counter moves, he's seen his snap count decrease with the additions of Joseph Ossai and David Bailey. In-division trades are rare, but not unheard of, and with McDonald still looking for an extension, some new scenery in New England could be helpful.

Pipe Dream Trade: WR Josh Downs, Indianapolis Colts

Realistic Trade: WR Calvin Ridley, Tennessee Titans

Downs pops up again as an ideal trade candidate, but this time we flip conferences and go to the current NFC No. 1 seed in San Francisco. The Niners' WR room looks like a graveyard right now, with WRs Mike Evans, Christian Kirk, Deebo Samuel and Demarcus Robinson all popping up on the injury report. If none of those guys are 100%, you're looking at a WR group of Jacob Cowing, Jordan Watkins and Brandin Cooks. Not exactly inspiring if you want to go win a Super Bowl.

Downs' ability to win with his route running and burst from the slot would give the Niners another option against man coverage and complements Evans really well when they'd both be on the field. Adding Downs helps round out the room and gives the Niners another option in a loaded offense, especially once everyone is healthy.

Calvin Ridley is a bit of a fascinating trade candidate at this point of his career. He's clearly not what he once was and has also been nursing an injury himself, but the hope is that a change of scenery gets the most out of him. He can win underneath and still has veteran savvy to help him get open.

Pipe Dream Trade: RB Jonathan Taylor, Indianapolis Colts

Realistic Trade: RB Tony Pollard, Tennessee Titans

The Vikings should be in the market for a running back at the deadline, whether it be a big splash or a smaller addition. Lost amidst the Kyler Murray disappointment talk is the fact that the Vikings can't run the ball consistently at all. Minnesota sits at 25th in EPA per play on all designed RB runs and 28th in rushing success rate on RB runs. On top of that, the Vikings' RBs don't make anyone miss; they sit tied with the Raiders for last in the NFL in avoided tackle rate, per TruMedia.

Part of that is the injuries to LG Donovan Jackson and TE Josh Oliver tanking the run game, but their running backs can't stay healthy either. Aaron Jones is more of a specialty third-down back at this stage, and Jordan Mason just came off of IR. Getting someone to take the lead in that room is huge for that offense.

Of all the Jonathan Taylor landing spots, Minnesota is the one I hope happens the most. This feels like the cleanest fit in terms of need, and Taylor combines the best of Mason and Jones as a runner. Getting Taylor's explosive capability and ability to make people miss would make the offense feel less congested, and maybe take some pressure off Murray.

If the Vikings miss out on Taylor, Tony Pollard wouldn't be a bad consolation prize. Pollard is playing some of his best ball this season, showing nice finishing ability on his runs along with his already impressive explosive capability. He can also be a factor in the receiving game, reducing how often you need to put Aaron Jones in.

Pipe Dream Trade: RB Breece Hall, New York Jets

Realistic Trade: DT Grover Stewart, Indianapolis Colts

It's no secret that the Giants are looking for a running back. Najee Harris is gone, and Cam Skattebo and Tyrone Tracy haven't inspired much confidence. The Giants currently sitting at 30th in success rate on all designed RB runs and 28th in explosive run rate. In an offense without a QB, having a run game that doesn't constantly put them behind the eight ball could give the Giants much more teeth as we enter the playoff push part of the season.

While I don't think a trade for Taylor makes sense for this team, I could see a move for Breece Hall if the Jets are willing to move on him. Hall has had issues staying healthy, but he's a big play machine who wins with burst and acceleration through lanes. He would make an offensive line that's played well shine even more while making offense just feel much easier for the QB.

However, a more realistic (and still very good) trade for the Giants would be a move for defensive tackle. The Giants have given up the eighth-highest EPA per carry on runs between the tackles, according to NFL Pro, and their 4.8 yards per carry allowed between the tackles is third-highest this season. Adding a veteran defensive tackle like Grover Stewart would immediately raise the floor of that run defense, with his ability to clog lanes giving LBs Arvell Reese and Tremaine Edmunds more chances to make plays in a completely clean run.

Pipe Dream Trade: EDGE Khalil Mack, Los Angeles Chargers

Realistic Trade: CB Donte Jackson, Los Angeles Chargers

The Panthers should be blowing the Chargers' phone up right now. Despite leading the NFC South, Carolina has taken two major hits to their playoff chances after getting physically overwhelmed by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Green Bay Packers. While their biggest issue probably isn't getting fixed with a trade at the deadline (offensive tackle), they can still try to revamp a defense that's been decimated by injury.

That's where the Chargers come in. If LA were to sell, the Panthers would be smart to go and pry some of their defenders away in hopes of making a playoff push.

Khalil Mack makes too much sense for the Panthers. I think his Chargers teammate Tuli Tuipulotu gets an extension from LA that keeps him around, but Mack is still a quality pass rusher and sets a physical edge. The Panthers' EDGE depth has been decimated by injury all season, but adding Mack would give them another veteran presence and more physical play.

If we move to the back end, where CBs Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson are injured, I think adding a veteran corner like Donte Jackson would make a ton of sense, too. He's played in a lot of schemes and is smart in zone coverage, which is what the Panthers major in. He also has experience playing inside and outside, which would give the Panthers plenty of options once Horn and Jackson potentially return to the starting defense.

Pipe Dream Trade: EDGE Khalil Mack, Los Angeles Chargers

Realistic Trade: CB Amik Robertson, Washington Commanders

A potential Khalil Mack return to Chicago would be a trade I'd be super excited for. The Bears did just trade for an impact player in DT Jeffrey Simmons, but adding another guy to that defensive line to help everyone fit a little better into their roles would help take the defense to a new level.

Montez Sweat had his best game this season in their Monday night win over the Seattle Seahawks, and Austin Booker has had more consistent flashes as a pass rusher, but getting a guy who sets a solid edge to rotate with Booker could be helpful. Mack coming back to Chicago would be a great story, but he would also round out the EDGE room in a big way.

A trade for a cornerback feels more likely, with CB Jaylon Johnson struggling and CB Tyrique Stevenson being more of a backup. Finding an outside corner would be paramount here, so a guy like the Titans' Alontae Taylor feels a bit out of the picture. Dolphins' CB JuJu Brents feels like a possibility, but Commanders' CB Amik Robertson feels like a guy that would fit on the outside opposite Johnson. He's aggressive and can disrupt receivers despite being undersized. He's played in man and zone concepts, but in Dennis Allen's defense, they can really turn him loose.

Pipe Dream Trade: CB Charvarius Ward, Indianapolis Colts

Realistic Trade: CB Amik Robertson, Washington Commanders

If you're reading this, the Lions still might need you to play cornerback. Their secondary has been the weakest part of the defense this season by a massive amount. Even though they got S Brian Branch back (and S Kerby Joseph has returned to practice), adding more cornerbacks to a room devastated by injury and poor play could help this defensive line transform from being very bad to at least passable for a playoff team.

The Colts' fire sale isn't limiting anyone, and Ward could be a player that the Lions add to give them needed experience in man coverage and production on the outside opposite DJ Reed. Ward has been in and out of the lineup since coming to Indy, but when he's healthy, he can still produce as an outside corner.

If the Colts don't feel like selling Ward, a reunion with Amik Robertson would make a lot of sense for both sides. Robertson knows the defense, can play inside and out and is a fan favorite. Bringing him back has to be considered in Detroit.

Pipe Dream Trade: OG Landon Dickerson, Philadelphia Eagles

Realistic Trade: RB Tyjae Spears, Tennessee Titans

For the Packers, the biggest addition they'll get is actually coming from inside the house. EDGE Micah Parsons is coming back to practice, adding one of the three best EDGE defenders in the NFL to the lineup. Once he gets back up to speed, the Green Bay defense should be dangerous.

However, the Packers' run game is simply mortifying. On all RB runs this season, Green Bay is 29th in explosive run rate and success rate, last in EPA per carry and 31st in yards before contact per carry. Giving this run game some life has to be the top priority at the deadline, and there are a couple of ways Green Bay can go about that.

The pie-in-the-sky dream would be to trade for Eagles guard Landon Dickerson. While Dickerson has dealt with injuries for the last two seasons, his physicality and productivity would help pry open run lanes for the Packers' rushing offense. Laken Tomlinson has played well after being a street free agent signing for Green Bay, but the spot at left guard has been a revolving door between Aaron Banks and Donovan Jennings, and nothing behind either door has been good. Adding Dickerson could help lift that run game in a big way.

If they can't swing a deal for Dickerson, adding an explosive back like Spears to the room could be really fun. Green Bay has six explosive runs this season and is behind the Miami Dolphins in tackle vvoided rate. Spears would give the room some much-needed juice and capability on third down as a receiver and pass blocker.

Pipe Dream Trade: EDGE Yaya Diaby, Tampa Bay Buccaneers

Realistic Trade: WR Josh Downs, Indianapolis Colts

Very quietly for the Seahawks, their EDGE depth has been rampaged by injury. EDGE Uchenna Nwosu missed the Monday night loss to the Bears with an ankle injury, and EDGE Dante Fowler has been subpar in his time with the Seahawks. Adding to the EDGE room might be a bit of a luxury given the state of the offense, but if they could swing for a guy like Diaby from the Bucs, it would round out that room in a big way.

Diaby plays with power and length, fitting the archetype of Mike Macdonald edges. Swinging a move for Diaby would allow the Seahawks to have a hockey lines situation of pass rushers waiting to make plays, much like their run to the Super Bowl last season. Then, if they want to get younger in the offseason, they can extend Diaby.

On the offensive side, finding someone that isn't all-world receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba to produce at receiver has been a big issue. WR Tory Horton has been in and out of the lineup with injuries, Cooper Kupp has been more of a dirty-work receiver at this point and Rashid Shaheed has been virtually nonexistent. Downs would give the Seahawks another separator who can win against multiple coverages, making offense feel a little less stressful.

Pipe Dream Trade: WR Brian Thomas Jr., Jacksonville Jaguars

Realistic Trade: CB Donte Jackson, Los Angeles Chargers

On the surface, the Rams' offense feels like they haven't really missed a beat. They're third in success rate, ninth in EPA per play and 10th in points per drive. However, their explosive play rate has dropped from 12.6% last year to 10.4% this year, and their explosive pass rate has dropped from 18.6% to 11.2%, a drastic falloff.

If the Rams are going to be without WR Davante Adams and TE Terrance Ferguson for the extent of this playoff push, the explosive plays in this offense are nonexistent. The Rams need someone to take the top off the defense consistently to open up underneath areas for WR Puka Nacua and the run game to thrive.

Brian Thomas Jr. would give the Rams some big-play ability in their offense. The Jaguars might not be keen on trading him at this point, but for the right price, I think they would entertain the idea. Thomas has been losing playing time in Jacksonville, but in Los Angeles he could be the stick of dynamite the Rams need while Adams and Ferguson are on IR.

On the flip side, the Rams' defense has been decimated by injury. While they get EDGE Myles Garrett back soon, CB Jaylen Watson is going to be out for the season with a shoulder injury. That leaves CB Trent McDuffie with…Emmanuel Forbes Jr and Josh Wallace at cornerback. For a team that wants to play multiple DBs on the field on money downs, going and getting another cornerback has to take priority. Jackson feels like the veteran presence the Rams normally go for in the secondary, with the ability to play multiple roles and thrive in off-coverage.

#2610. Biggest MLB offseason questions: How long will lockout last? Will we see a free agency frenzy?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Not so long ago, the Milwaukee Brewers were crowned World Series champions, and at the moment of the last out, the 2026-27 Major League offseason began. So let's talk about that.

The winter ahead is one shot through with uncertainty, as labor strife figures to roil the sport and perhaps even compromise the 2027 season. Those matters, vital as they are, won't be the only story, and we'll still have the familiar presences of free agency and trade talk to sustain us.

To set the scene for all that's ahead in advance of the 2027 campaign – good, ill, or somewhere in the middle – we're here to take a look at the five questions that will inform an offseason that's going to be quite unusual and – for good, ill, or somewhere in the middle – probably unforgettable. Let's explore those five queries right now …

The current collective bargaining agreement – or CBA, the accord that governs the working relationship between clubs/owners and players – is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1 of this year. At that time, MLB owners are all but certain to lock out the players. That's a labor stoppage, and that means the offseason will be brought to a sudden halt. The lockout, the purpose of which is to preempt a players' strike, will last until a new CBA is agreed to. Agreeing to a new CBA will be no simple matter, and owners and their hireling, commissioner Rob Manfred, are pushing for a cap on team payrolls. The players, as represented by their union, the MLBPA, have never shown any willingness to agree to a cap-and-floor system. There are a lot of other issues to iron out, as the CBA is an all-encompassing document, but the fight over a cap will be what drags out the lockout.

The heart of the matter is whether the lockout will last long enough to push back, abbreviate, or – perish the thought – cancel entirely the 2027 season. The latter is the worst-case scenario and is highly unlikely, but it's a possibility, however remote. More of a threat is a 2027 season that doesn't span the usual 162 games.

We have a recent precedent to guide us. The last time the CBA was up for negotiation during the offseason of 2021-22, owners locked out the players for 99 days. That meant a shortened spring training by about two and a half weeks and forced the regular season calendar to be compressed, albeit while still preserving the 162-game docket. As such, we can say that if the lockout lasts beyond the middle of March 2027, then we'll likely lose regular-season games.

For further context, here's a brief history of modern labor stoppages in the sport:

Just two, the 1981 and 1994-95 player strikes, significantly compromised seasons. The 1994-95 stoppage cost us the 1994 World Series, and it took years for the sport to recover from the resulting fan disaffection.

As for the 2027 season, the worst-case scenario may not be the loss of the entire season but rather the loss of 60 games off the regular-season slate. Here's the explanation from our recent Lockout 101 piece:

"… [I]f the lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That matters because Manfred and the league hope to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation in 2028. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. This amounts to a major incentive, at least on the league side, to agree to a new CBA before June arrives."

Obviously, the hope is that the lockout doesn't even affect the spring training calendar, let alone cost us a major chunk of the regular season.

As noted, the big fight is over whether or not MLB will have a cap-and-floor structure moving forward, as is the case in the NFL, NBA, and NHL. Owners have tied every single proposal wrinkle to date to the players' acceptance of a cap. However, it remains highly unlikely, at least until further notice, that the union would ever agree to such a thing.

The other major issue is a likely restructuring of the revenue-sharing system. Specifically, the next CBA is highly likely to revise the system so that local broadcast revenues are shared much more evenly. Fortunately, there's already some common ground on this issue, and a reordering of that system would directly address the revenue disparities within MLB that are such a reliable source of consternation – and misinformation – without the grievous labor war that a continued cap push would force upon us.

Otherwise, some other key wrinkles and changes may come out of the wash. That list potentially includes:

This doesn't get into evergreen matters like an increase in the minimum salary, draft bonus pools, the qualifying offer system, active roster sizes, and so forth. There's a lot to sort out, to say the least. The expectation is that the next CBA is going to lead to sweeping changes to the sport starting in 2027 and, perhaps by design, growing over time. Even if there's no cap and floor, the economic structure of MLB is almost certain to look very different after this winter.

Overall, this is one of the weakest free agent classes in living memory, but there is elite superstar value to be found at the tip-top with back-to-back (for the moment) American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal.

Skubal, who turns 30 on Nov. 20, remains foremost in the discussion for best pitcher in baseball, and he's going to be paid like it. The expectation is that he'll wind up signing the largest pitcher contract in MLB history and perhaps also fetch the highest-ever annual salary for a pitcher. It's not out of the question that Skubal's next contract could approach or even surpass $400 million in total value. At those rates, the incumbent Los Angeles Dodgers and the free-spending New York Mets are the consensus favorites. The Chicago Cubs are also reportedly heavily interested in Skubal, and surprise bidders are always possible. Other notable free agent names include Freddy Peralta, Michael King, Jazz Chisholm Jr., Trevor Rogers, Adrian Morejon, and Teruaki Sato. Our ranking of the top 50 2026-27 free agents has you covered.

The "when" of all this is more complicated thanks to the upcoming lockout detailed above. Will premium free agents and their representatives rush to find some stability in advance of the stoppage, during which no major-league transactions will be permitted, or will they decide that the long game will be better for their markets? It's possible that the biggest spenders on the team side will look to make moves early, as the barrel of the next CBA figures to be leveled directly at them and their abundant revenues. Or maybe the unknown will have a chilling effect on spending before we arrive at the lockout.

The past is not always prelude, but let's note that we saw a flurry of spending leading up to the lockout of 2021-22. Indeed, in November 2021, MLB teams committed more than $1.7 billion to free agents prior to the lockout. The Texas Rangers alone guaranteed $500 million to a new middle infield – Corey Seager and Marcus Semien – before the lockout put an end to such things. In all, teams put ink to paper on five nine-figure contracts prior to the 2021-22 lockout.

The comparisons may not entirely hold since this upcoming CBA should bring about a much more drastic re-ordering of the sport than the current expiring CBA did. As such, teams may proceed cautiously given all the uncertainties. Or, as just mentioned, they may seek to get business done before the ways of doing business change entirely. We'll see soon enough. If we do see the dollars start flying before the lockout, then the upcoming Nov. 10-12 general managers meetings in Las Vegas may occasion the groundwork for all those deals.

Will a lackluster free agent class mean more headline-grabbing trades? That may indeed be answered in the affirmative this winter. Yes, the CBA uncertainty will have a bearing on trades, especially those that involve the assumption of major salary obligations, but big trades still figure to be a prominent part of this offseason.

It's of course impossible to know who's going to be dealt ahead of time, but some big names perhaps on the move this winter include Francisco Lindor, Mason Miller, Spencer Strider, Hunter Greene, Otto Lopez, Jeremy Peña, Ketel Marte, Jacob deGrom, and of course others. Paul Skenes? Almost certainly not, but you'll just as certainly hear his name bandied about.

Turning back to last lockout, it was mostly minor trades before the sport shut down. Yes, we'll see big ones this time around, but they may not happen until we have a new CBA in place and the lockout is over.

Let's make time for the losers, shall we? The teams that didn't make the postseason in 2026 and otherwise qualify will take part in the draft lottery, which is presently scheduled for Dec. 8. That lottery will determine which teams get the top six picks in the 2027 MLB Draft.

This year, 16 of the 18 non-playoff teams will be in the lottery. Non-playoff teams can be barred from the lottery if they've had lottery picks in two consecutive seasons. If a team is a revenue-sharing payor, then it can't be in the lottery in consecutive years. Those wrinkles this year mean that the San Francisco Giants and Pittsburgh Pirates will not be in the lottery and can't pick higher than 10th in the 2027 Draft.

Here's how the preliminary lottery odds look for those 16 teams in the mix, based on how they finished the 2026 season:

It's too soon to know which players will be in the mix for that top pick since the amateur seasons haven't begun yet. However, two early favorites to go No. 1 are University of Florida shortstop Brendan Lawson and Mississippi State left-hander Tomas Valinicius.

#2609. Should the NBA shorten games to 40 minutes? Pros and cons of move as league battles early season injury crisis

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Opinions vary on the causes and potential solutions for the NBA's early-season injury crisis, and an idea commissioner Adam Silver once floated is back in the conversation. Sports Illustrated's Chris Mannix said on the Open Floor podcast that he has heard that Silver likes the idea of shortening NBA games to 40 minutes. This is an idea that Silver has previously supported publicly.

"As we get more involved in global basketball, the NBA is the only league that plays 48 minutes. And I would be -- I am -- a fan of four 10-minute quarters," Silver said on The Dan Patrick Show in 2025. "I'm not sure that many others are. Putting aside what it means for records and things like that, yeah, I think that a two-hour format for a game is more consistent with modern television habits."

Silver is not the only major supporter of the idea. Mark Cuban has vouched for it as well, and given the sheer number of notable injuries the NBA has endured so far this season, the league is suddenly in a position in which it probably needs to consider pretty drastic changes to keep its best players on the floor. Is the idea of a 40-minute NBA game feasible? What are the pros and cons here, and why do the negatives ultimately outweigh the positives? Let's dive in.

Some basic math: 82 48-minute games equals 3,936 minutes of regular-season basketball for every team, before overtime. Trim games to 40 minutes and teams instead play 3,280 regular-season minutes per year, or around 17% less total basketball. Fewer minutes means fewer opportunities for players to get hurt.

That much is essentially indisputable. Where things get more promising is in the theoretical, compounding effect of playing less. If players are likelier to get hurt when they're overworked, reducing their workloads could potentially limit those more vulnerable minutes late in games and seasons because they simply aren't accumulating the same degree of wear and tear.

Fresher players would hopefully be healthier players.

College basketball games are 40 minutes. WNBA games are 40 minutes. FIBA games are 40 minutes. The NBA is the outlier here. It is the only major basketball league in which games have those eight extra minutes, and standardizing games across the sport could make it easier to translate player production across leagues.

This isn't strictly a basketball phenomenon, either. Major League Baseball is in the middle of a renaissance sparked in part by game-shortening measures like the pitch clock. Silver acknowledged this in that Dan Patrick Show interview, calling a two-hour game "more consistent with modern television habits." It's simply easier to hold the attention span of a television audience for a 40-minute game than a 48-minute game.

This has certainly been less true in the "eight champions in eight years" era we are currently living through, but the NBA tends to be more predictable than other sports when it comes to playoff outcomes. The NFL's single-elimination format makes the best teams extremely vulnerable in the postseason, and baseball is so inherently volatile because pitcher performance makes upsets so common.

Over a seven-game sample, the better team usually wins out in an NBA playoff series. This isn't absolute, of course, especially with health and 3-point variance factored in, but Cinderella runs are relatively rare in basketball. Only two NBA champions were seeded lower than No. 3 in their conference, and neither came this century. Nearly twice as many No. 1 seeds (53) have won titles than all other seeds combined (27).

Smaller samples create more volatility. It's easier for an inferior team to overcome a superior one across 40 minutes than it is across 48. Every hot shooting stretch means more; every key player in foul trouble has to miss a larger portion of the game. If you view the NBA through a purely competitive lens, this is a negative. If you view the NBA primarily as an entertainment product, creating more upsets is a real benefit of shortening games.

NBA games may last 48 minutes, but nobody actually plays anywhere near that much anymore. In fact, nobody even averages 40 minutes per game anymore, with Jamal Murray leading the league at 38.4 minutes per game thus far this season. What this essentially means is that teams could largely maintain the workloads of their superstars in a 40-minute game and simply use their bench players less.

This is the immediate reason that a change like this isn't feasible. Why on Earth would the NBA Players Association go along with a change that trivializes the majority of its membership? Stars would suddenly be more valuable than ever because they'd be playing a greater proportion of the game, but everyone else becomes less valuable for the same reason.

This has enormous team-building implications as well. Suddenly, superteams would be back in vogue because tying all of your money and assets into two or three players would make more sense in a world where fewer players are needed to get through a game or season.

On this note, it's not even clear what sort of health benefits this change would actually create. Bench players would certainly stay healthier just for playing less... but would stars benefit from this at all? That's less clear, and the NBA is obviously far more invested in keeping the best players on the court than role players.

There are theoretical fixes here, but none are perfect. The NBA could put a minutes cap on individual players, but remember, stoppages aren't uniform. Say the league sets a 30-minute cap, and a player crosses that threshold because no timeout, foul or dead-ball turnover stops the game for him to leave. How does the league handle that? It could mandate that players sit one full quarter, but doing so would inevitably lead to star players essentially playing at least one full half.

There's no clean solution to this problem, and until someone finds one, it's hard to believe this sort of change is feasible.

The length of games is only a small component of what makes the NBA schedule so grueling. Shortening games to 40 minutes wouldn't eliminate the need to travel to 41 regular-season road games. It wouldn't remove back-to-backs from the slate either, and it wouldn't bake more time into the schedule for practice, conditioning or a longer training camp.

NBA basketball is simply more difficult to play today than it was in the past. Players are more skilled and athletic than they used to be, forcing them to cover more space, play faster and endure more punishment than they once did. Shortening the game wouldn't change how it is played.

That's the danger of any incremental solution. Shortening games would carry substantial costs to the NBA. Shorter games would mean fewer commercial breaks for the television product. If the league tries it and it doesn't work, it has sacrificed revenue for nothing and is therefore less likely to take bigger financial risks to reap more substantial rewards, such as cutting games from the schedule.

Even if records and statistics aren't that important in the grand scheme of things, they're treated as sacred components of league history by many fans. Even if every other major rule has been subject to change across eras, the length of the game has been stable. That makes comparing stats and records across history at least somewhat viable. That changes if you shorten the game. Modern records become nearly unbreakable.

If the league were willing to tamper with its history in this way, there are simply lower-risk changes it could make instead of shortening games. One concept: increasing the value of 3-pointers to four points and similarly pushing 2s up to three. Doing this would narrow the value gap between shots behind the arc and those inside it, thereby incentivizing players to take more mid-range shots and, theoretically, forcing defenders to cover less ground than they do currently. One reason a change like this is unlikely is that it would make comparing numbers across eras pointless.

The NBA may one day decide it's willing to break that glass, but it has given no indication that it is prepared to do so now.

Coming off a bye, Houston should be getting it together on that side of the ball, and there's no better opponent to do it against.

Amid the Chargers' disastrous year, the defense has actually played well: seventh in EPA per play and 10th in success rate. They defend the middle of the field — where C.J. Stroud likes to attack — well. The Texans struggle to run the ball and struggle to cash in in the red zone. That sounds like a recipe for an UNDER to me.

Cincinnati's defense is actually OK down to down but allows a ton of big plays. And when we hear "allows a ton of big plays," we like OVER on yardage totals.

All eyes will be on Bijan Robinson after a quiet couple of weeks, but really, I think this could be a huge Drake London game. Here's why: Cincinnati cannot defend the middle of the field whatsoever. On passes between the numbers, the Bengals have allowed

That's exactly where Drake London thrives. From Weeks 3-7, which eliminates the two games Cooper Rush started and last week's game against the Buccaneers in a torrential downpour, London had the seventh-most yards in the NFL on throws between the numbers. As long as Penix is playing (he is) and there isn't crazy rain (there isn't projected to be), London should take advantage of a great matchup Sunday. Add in that the Falcons are going to have to throw to keep up, and the volume should absolutely be there, too.

The Phillies will seek a left-handed setup man this offseason, reports The Athletic. Philadelphia has Tanner Banks and Tim Mayza, though both are middle-innings lefties more than high-leverage relievers. Manager Don Mattingly's late-inning unit is all righties at the moment: Jonathan Bowlan, Caleb Kilian, Jhoan Duran, and Alex McFarlane.

We ranked four lefty relievers among our top 50 free agents: Adrian Morejon (No. 2), JoJo Romero (No. 31), Alex Vesia (No. 35), and Kris Bubic (No. 45). Morejon and Bubic may get opportunities to start next season. Other free agent lefties include Tim Hill, A.J. MInter, Sean Newcomb, Steven Okert, AJ Puk, and former Phillie Gregory Soto.

The Yankees need almost an entirely new bullpen this offseason, and they have interest in re-signing setup man Paul Blackburn, according to the New York Daily News. New York tendered closer David Bednar the $23.15 million qualifying offer and seems likely to get him back, either on the QO or on a multi-year deal, but they will need to improve the setup crew regardless.

We ranked Blackburn as the No. 33 free agent this offseason. He had a terrific season with the Yankees in 2026, his first year as a full-time reliever. The Yankees have shown the ability to drum up quality relievers almost out of nowhere. They tend to let those guys leave as free agents, then build up someone else to replace them. This happened when Blackburn replaced Luke Weaver.

Among their list of wants this offseason, the Marlins will look to add to their rotation and bullpen, as well as a corner bat, reports the Miami Herald. That corner bat could be at first base, third base, left or right fields. Sandy Alcantara and Eury Pérez are the only locks for Miami's rotation, though Max Meyer should be ready to go next season following this year's neck injury.

Gold Glove finalist Javier Sanoja filled in at third base capably this year, though he fits best as a super utility man who plays all over. Owen Caissie, Griffin Conine, and Heriberto Hernández are Miami's corner outfield options, and Kyle Stowers moved from the outfield to first base in 2026. There are opportunities to improve aplenty for the Marlins.
